about: Economics (ECON0002) is UCL's 30-credit, year-long (Terms 1 and 2) first course in micro and macroeconomics, compulsory for first-year BSc Economics students and for several joint degrees including Philosophy and Economics, Economics and Geography, and PPE (Economics and Politics concentration). The 2026/27 catalogue describes it as starting from historical and cross-country facts about growth, inequality and stability and then building analytical micro and macro concepts: decision-making by economic actors, goods, labour and credit markets, institutions, market success and failure, and fiscal and monetary policy. UCL's first-year programme has been built around CORE's free textbook The Economy (UCL news, 2021), and this pack follows a CORE-style approach. Per the 2026/27 catalogue, assessment is 80% exams (two assessments) and 20% coursework; no week-by-week syllabus is published there, so topics follow the catalogue's content list.
topics: Historical and cross-country growth, inequality, stability
Core concepts of micro and macroeconomics
Institutions as the rules of the game
Sources of market success and failure
Households and firms in the aggregate economy

notes.h: Growth, inequality and stability across history and countries
notes.body:
A CORE-style course begins with the facts that economics has to explain: why living standards rose so suddenly in some places, why incomes are so unequal, and why economies are periodically unstable.

The hockey stick of living standards
- For most of history GDP per head grew extremely slowly. In Britain sustained growth began around the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries with the Industrial Revolution; other countries took off later, some only in the twentieth century.
- Plotted over a thousand years, GDP per head looks like a hockey stick: flat for centuries, then sharply upward.
- Before the take-off, economies were close to a Malthusian trap: when technology raised output, population grew and income per head returned towards subsistence.
- The take-off is linked to the "capitalist revolution": private property, markets and firms combined with a permanent stream of new technology.

Measuring and comparing growth
- GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced in an economy in a period. Real GDP adjusts for price changes; GDP per head divides by population.
- Comparisons between countries use purchasing power parity (PPP) to allow for differences in price levels.
- Growth compounds. A rough rule of 70: a variable growing at g% a year doubles in about 70/g years. At 2% a year income doubles in about 35 years (1.02 to the power 35 ≈ 2.0); at 7% a year, in about 10.
- Ratio (logarithmic) scales show constant growth rates as straight lines, which makes growth across centuries readable.

Divergence and convergence
- Countries that took off early pulled far ahead, so the gaps in GDP per head between rich and poor countries became enormous.
- Some economies (Japan after 1950, South Korea, more recently China) grew fast enough to catch up substantially; others did not. Institutions, policies and history help explain the difference.

Inequality
- The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income received against the cumulative share of the population, ranked from poorest. Perfect equality is the 45-degree line.
- The Gini coefficient equals the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the whole area under the equality line. It runs from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has everything).
- Worked example: four people earn 10, 20, 30 and 40. Cumulative income shares are 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0. The area under the Lorenz curve is 0.375, so the Gini is 1 − 2 × 0.375 = 0.25. If one person had all 40, the Gini would be 0.75, the maximum for four people, (n − 1)/n.
- Inequality differs between countries and over time, and taxes and transfers reduce it: the Gini for disposable income is lower than for market income in rich countries.

Stability
- Economies grow unevenly. Output fluctuates around its trend in business cycles, and occasionally collapses: the Great Depression of the 1930s, the global financial crisis of 2008, and the pandemic contraction of 2020.
- Inflation has varied as well: the UK experienced very high inflation in the 1970s, low and stable inflation after the Bank of England was given operational independence in 1997, and a surge to 11.1% (CPI) in October 2022.

Exam tips: use growth rates and doubling times to make comparisons vivid, explain how a Gini is calculated rather than just quoting it, and link each fact to the models the course later uses to explain it.

notes.h: Thinking like an economist: scarcity, choice and models
notes.body:
Economics studies how people interact with each other and with the natural environment in producing their livelihoods. A few concepts recur in every part of the course.

Scarcity and opportunity cost
- Something is scarce when having more of it means having less of something else that we value.
- The opportunity cost of an action is the value of the next best alternative given up. An hour spent studying has an opportunity cost of the free time (or the wage) forgone.
- Economic cost includes opportunity costs, not just money spent. Economic rent is the payoff from an action minus the payoff from the next best alternative.

Models
- A model is a deliberately simplified description that isolates the mechanisms we care about. Ceteris paribus ("other things equal") means holding other factors constant to see the effect of one change.
- Good models make predictions that can be tested against data.

Preferences: indifference curves
- An indifference curve joins combinations of two goods (for example consumption and free time) that give the same utility.
- Curves further from the origin represent higher utility; they slope downward because both goods are valued, and they are usually convex because people value a good more when they have little of it.
- The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) is the amount of one good a person is willing to give up for one more unit of the other while staying equally well off: the slope of the indifference curve.

Constraints: the feasible frontier
- The feasible frontier (or budget constraint) shows the combinations that are attainable. For a worker with hourly wage w and 24 hours, consumption c = w(24 − t), where t is free time.
- Its slope is the marginal rate of transformation (MRT): how much of one good must be given up to get one more unit of the other. Here MRT = w.

Constrained choice
- The best feasible choice is where the highest attainable indifference curve just touches the frontier: MRS = MRT.
- Example: with utility u = c × t, the MRS between free time and consumption is c/t. Setting c/t = w and c = w(24 − t) gives t = 12 hours and c = 12w. This person chooses 12 hours of free time whatever the wage, because the income and substitution effects cancel exactly.

Income and substitution effects
- A higher wage raises the opportunity cost of free time, so the substitution effect reduces free time.
- It also makes the person richer, and if free time is a normal good the income effect increases it.
- The overall effect on hours worked is therefore ambiguous. Over the long run, working hours have fallen as wages rose, which suggests the income effect has often dominated.

Marginal thinking
Decisions are made at the margin: compare the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost. Choose more of an activity while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.

Microeconomics and macroeconomics
- Microeconomics studies the decisions of individuals, firms and governments and how they interact in particular markets.
- Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: total output, employment, inflation and the effects of fiscal and monetary policy. It cannot simply add up individual behaviour, because of feedback effects such as the paradox of thrift.

Positive and normative
Positive statements describe how the economy works and can be tested; normative statements are about what ought to be and involve value judgements about fairness or efficiency.

Exam tips: always label diagrams (axes, curves, the optimum), state the MRS = MRT condition in words, and say which effect dominates when you discuss a price or wage change.

notes.h: How economic actors decide: strategic interaction, firms and employment
notes.body:
Households, firms, workers, banks and governments make decisions that affect each other. The course models these using game theory and the economics of the firm.

Game theory basics
- A game has players, strategies and payoffs. A best response is the strategy that gives a player the highest payoff given what the others do.
- A dominant strategy is a best response whatever the others do.
- A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies, one per player, in which each is a best response to the others: nobody can gain by changing strategy alone.

The prisoners' dilemma
- Each player has a dominant strategy (defect), but when both defect they are worse off than if both had co-operated. The Nash equilibrium is not Pareto efficient.
- Many social dilemmas take this form: over-fishing, climate change, arms races, price wars between firms.

Public goods games and social preferences
- In a typical experiment, each of four players gets 20 tokens and decides how many to put in a common pot; the pot is multiplied by 1.6 and shared equally. Each token contributed returns only 0.4 to the contributor, so contributing nothing is a dominant strategy for a purely self-interested player.
- If all contribute everything, each ends with 32; a player who contributes nothing while the others give everything gets 44.
- In experiments (for example Fehr and Gächter, 2000) contributions start well above zero and decline over repeated rounds, but stay high when players can pay to punish free riders. People are not purely selfish: altruism, reciprocity and inequality aversion matter.

The firm and its customers
- A firm selling a differentiated product chooses its price facing a downward-sloping demand curve.
- Profit is maximised where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC), the point where an isoprofit curve is tangent to the demand curve.
- The markup over cost depends on the price elasticity of demand: (P − MC)/P = 1/|ε|. With an elasticity of −2, the price is twice marginal cost; with −4, the markup is 25% of the price. Less elastic demand (fewer close substitutes) means higher markups.
- Price is above marginal cost, so some trades that would benefit both sides do not happen: there is a deadweight loss compared with a competitive outcome.

The firm and its employees
- Employment contracts are incomplete: the firm cannot specify or enforce effort fully. This is a principal–agent problem.
- The worker's employment rent is the value of the job minus the value of the next best alternative (the reservation option, including unemployment benefits and the chance of finding another job).
- Firms pay above the reservation wage so that losing the job is costly, which motivates effort; this is an efficiency wage. Higher unemployment raises the cost of job loss, so firms can get the same effort for a lower wage.

Other actors
- Banks decide whom to lend to and on what terms, facing their own information problem: borrowers know more about their projects and effort than lenders.
- Governments and central banks also act strategically, anticipating how households and firms respond.

Exam tips: for a game, write out the payoff matrix, underline best responses and then identify the Nash equilibria; for a firm, link the markup to the elasticity and explain the resulting deadweight loss.

notes.h: Markets for goods, labour and credit
notes.body:
Markets co-ordinate millions of decisions. The course studies three kinds: goods markets, the labour market and the credit market.

Competitive goods markets
- When buyers and sellers are price-takers, the demand curve shows the quantity buyers want at each price and the supply curve shows what firms will sell (marginal cost).
- Equilibrium is where they cross. Example: demand P = 100 − Q and supply P = 20 + Q give Q = 40 and P = 60.
- Consumer surplus is the area between the demand curve and the price; producer surplus is the area between the price and the supply curve. In the example each is ½ × 40 × 40 = 800.
- Shifts: a rise in income shifts demand for a normal good right, raising price and quantity; a cost increase shifts supply left, raising price and lowering quantity.
- Price elasticity of demand: the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price. At the example's equilibrium it is −1 × (60/40) = −1.5.

Taxes and incidence
- A £10 per-unit tax on sellers shifts supply up to P = 30 + Q, so Q = 35, buyers pay £65 and sellers keep £55.
- Tax revenue is 10 × 35 = £350. Consumer and producer surplus fall to 612.5 each, and the deadweight loss is ½ × 10 × 5 = 25.
- Who bears a tax depends on elasticities, not on who legally pays it: the less elastic side bears more. Here the two slopes are equal, so the burden is split evenly.

The labour market
- Firms set prices as a markup on costs, which fixes the real wage they can pay: the price-setting curve, horizontal in a simple model.
- The wage-setting curve gives the real wage firms must pay to secure effort at each level of employment; it slopes upwards because lower unemployment makes job loss less costly.
- Labour market equilibrium is where the two curves cross. Involuntary unemployment remains even in equilibrium, because it is what disciplines effort.
- Policies that increase competition (lower markups) shift the price-setting curve up, raising real wages and employment. More generous unemployment benefits shift the wage-setting curve up.
- Minimum wages: at the time of writing (October 2026), the National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over is £12.71 an hour, in force from 1 April 2026 (up from £12.21); check GOV.UK for later rates.

The credit market
- Borrowing and lending let households move consumption between periods. People who are impatient, or who expect higher future income, borrow; others save.
- The interest rate is the price of bringing consumption forward: borrowing £100 today at 5% means giving up £105 next year.
- Lenders face information problems: they cannot observe how carefully borrowers will use the money. They respond by requiring collateral (wealth) and by credit rationing, so people without wealth may be excluded or pay higher rates. This can reinforce inequality.
- Banks create money when they make loans, by crediting the borrower's deposit account. The central bank sets the short-term policy rate, and banks' lending rates are set as a markup over it, reflecting risk and costs.

Exam tips: draw the diagram for every market question, mark surpluses and deadweight loss as triangles with their values, and remember that tax incidence depends on relative elasticities.

notes.h: Institutions: the rules of the game
notes.body:
Douglass North, in Institutions, Institutional Change and Economic Performance (1990), described institutions as the rules of the game in a society. They include laws, property rights, contracts and social norms, and they determine who does what, who gets what and how much bargaining power each party has.

Why institutions matter
- The same technology and resources can produce very different outcomes under different rules. Rules decide what is feasible and what is chosen.
- The capitalist revolution depended on institutions: private property, enforceable contracts, markets and firms.
- Differences in institutions help explain why some countries grew rich. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001) argued that institutions set up by colonisers had long-lasting effects on income; the three shared the 2024 Nobel memorial prize in economics for work on how institutions affect prosperity.

Allocations, power and bargaining
- An allocation describes the outcome of an interaction: who does what work and who receives what.
- Power is the ability to do and get the things we want in opposition to the intentions of others. It can come from setting the terms of an exchange (take-it-or-leave-it power) or from being able to impose costs on others.
- When one party can make a take-it-or-leave-it offer, they can push the other down to their reservation option and capture all the economic rent.
- Changing the rules, for example legislation limiting working hours or giving workers a say, shifts the outcome along the set of efficient allocations.

Pareto efficiency
- An allocation is Pareto dominated if another feasible allocation makes at least one person better off and nobody worse off.
- An allocation is Pareto efficient if no such alternative exists.
- There are usually many Pareto-efficient allocations, some very unequal. Efficiency says nothing about fairness: an allocation in which one person gets everything can be Pareto efficient.

Fairness
- Substantive judgements look at the outcome itself (income, happiness, freedom).
- Procedural judgements look at how the outcome was reached: through voluntary exchange, fair competition or force.
- A veil-of-ignorance thought experiment (John Rawls, A Theory of Justice, 1971) asks which rules you would choose without knowing your own position in society.

Evidence from the ultimatum game
- A proposer offers a split of a sum; the responder accepts (both get the split) or rejects (both get nothing).
- A purely self-interested responder should accept any positive offer, so a self-interested proposer offers the smallest amount.
- In experiments, proposers commonly offer between 40% and 50%, and responders often reject offers below about 20% to 30%, even though rejecting costs them money. Social norms of fairness and reciprocity shape bargaining.

Rules and efficiency
- Well-designed rules can turn social dilemmas into co-operation: enforceable contracts, regulation, and community norms with punishment of free riders.
- Badly designed or extractive rules can leave potential gains from trade unrealised or channel them to a powerful few.

Exam tips: when discussing a change in the rules, ask two separate questions, whether the outcome is Pareto efficient and whether it is fair, and support each with a diagram or evidence.

notes.h: When markets work and when they fail
notes.body:
Competitive markets can co-ordinate the actions of strangers remarkably well, but they also fail in predictable ways. Knowing which applies is central to policy.

When markets succeed
- Adam Smith (The Wealth of Nations, 1776) described the "invisible hand": self-interested trade can promote the general good.
- In a competitive equilibrium with no externalities and full information, every trade with value above cost happens, total surplus is maximised and the allocation is Pareto efficient (the first welfare theorem).
- Prices carry information: a rise in price signals scarcity and gives buyers a reason to economise and sellers a reason to produce more.

Market failure
A market fails when the allocation it produces is Pareto inefficient. The main causes are:

1. External effects (externalities)
- A negative externality is a cost imposed on others that the decision-maker does not pay, such as pollution. The marginal social cost exceeds the marginal private cost, so the market overproduces.
- Example: demand P = 100 − Q, private marginal cost 20 + Q and an external cost of £10 per unit. The market produces 40 units, but the efficient quantity, where 100 − Q = 30 + Q, is 35. The deadweight loss of over-production is ½ × 10 × 5 = £25.
- A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external damage (named after Arthur Pigou, The Economics of Welfare, 1920) makes the polluter face the full cost. Here a £10 tax per unit achieves Q = 35.
- Other remedies: quotas or bans; tradable permits (the UK Emissions Trading Scheme, launched in 2021); and private bargaining, which Ronald Coase (The Problem of Social Cost, 1960) showed can reach efficiency if property rights are clear and bargaining costs are low. In practice bargaining costs are often high and many people are affected.
- Positive externalities, such as vaccination or research, are under-produced; subsidies are the matching remedy.

2. Public goods and common-pool resources
- A public good is non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people cannot be stopped from using it), such as street lighting or national defence. Markets under-supply it because people can free ride.
- Common-pool resources, such as fisheries, are rival but non-excludable and tend to be overused. Elinor Ostrom (Governing the Commons, 1990) showed that communities can sometimes manage them through local rules, monitoring and sanctions.

3. Asymmetric information
- Hidden attributes cause adverse selection: George Akerlof's "market for lemons" (1970) showed that if buyers cannot tell good used cars from bad, good cars may be withdrawn and the market can unravel. Health insurance faces the same problem.
- Hidden actions cause moral hazard: insured people may take less care, and workers may shirk.
- Remedies include compulsory insurance, warranties, screening and regulation.

4. Market power
- A firm with market power sets price above marginal cost, so quantity is below the efficient level and there is a deadweight loss. Competition policy and regulation address this.

Government failure
Intervention can also fail: policymakers lack information, are lobbied by interest groups, or create new distortions. Compare imperfect markets with imperfect governments.

UK examples
- The single-use carrier bag charge in England (5p from October 2015, raised to 10p in May 2021) targets a negative externality.
- The Soft Drinks Industry Levy, introduced in April 2018, taxes sugary drinks by sugar content, partly to change recipes.

Exam tips: for every policy question, name the market failure, show the gap between private and social cost or benefit on a diagram, and assess at least two remedies.

notes.h: The aggregate economy: households, firms and fluctuations
notes.body:
Macroeconomics looks at how the decisions of households and firms add up to total output, employment and inflation, and why the economy fluctuates.

Measuring the economy
- GDP can be measured by output (value added), expenditure or income; in principle all three agree.
- The expenditure identity: Y = C + I + G + X − M (consumption, investment, government purchases, exports minus imports).
- Real GDP growth is the main measure of the business cycle; a recession is often defined as two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP.

Households: consumption smoothing
- Households prefer a steady path of consumption to large swings, because of diminishing marginal utility.
- If they can borrow and save, they base consumption on expected lifetime (permanent) income, so temporary shocks to income have small effects on consumption.
- In practice many households are credit-constrained or hold little wealth, so their spending tracks current income closely. Weak confidence also raises precautionary saving.

Firms: investment
- Investment in machinery, buildings and inventories depends on expected profitability, the cost of borrowing and confidence. It is much more volatile than consumption and drives much of the business cycle.

The multiplier
- An initial rise in spending raises incomes, which raises consumption, which raises incomes again.
- In the simplest model with marginal propensity to consume c, the multiplier is 1/(1 − c). With c = 0.8 it is 5.
- Taxes and imports leak spending out of the circular flow. With tax rate t and marginal propensity to import m, the multiplier is 1/(1 − c(1 − t) + m). With c = 0.8, t = 0.25 and m = 0.2, it is 1/0.6 ≈ 1.67, which is far more realistic.
- Aggregate demand is the total of planned spending; the goods market is in equilibrium where output equals aggregate demand.

The paradox of thrift
If all households try to save more at the same time, spending falls, so output and incomes fall, and total saving may not rise at all. What makes sense for one household can backfire for the economy as a whole.

Unemployment and output
- When aggregate demand falls, firms cut production and employment, so unemployment rises above its equilibrium level. Okun's law describes this negative link between output growth and changes in unemployment.
- In the medium run, the labour market model (wage-setting and price-setting curves) determines equilibrium unemployment.

Inflation and the Phillips curve
- When unemployment is below its equilibrium level, workers' bargaining power rises and firms raise prices, so inflation increases. When unemployment is above it, inflation falls.
- The original Phillips curve (A. W. Phillips, 1958) found a negative relationship between unemployment and wage inflation in UK data. Once people come to expect inflation, the short-run trade-off shifts: holding unemployment below equilibrium leads to ever-rising inflation.
- Supply shocks, such as the energy price rises of 2022 and the motor-fuel-driven rise in 2026, raise inflation and can lower output at the same time.

Current UK picture (at the time of writing, October 2026; check the latest ONS release)
- CPI inflation was 3.5% in the year to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August; motor fuels made the largest upward contribution (ONS, 21 October 2026). CPIH was 3.6%.

Exam tips: show multiplier calculations step by step, explain why leakages make the multiplier smaller, and distinguish shocks to demand from shocks to supply when explaining inflation.

Governments and central banks try to keep output close to its potential and inflation low and stable. In the UK, monetary policy is set by the Bank of England and fiscal policy by HM Treasury, with independent forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Monetary policy in the UK
- The Bank of England has had operational independence since 1997. The Chancellor sets the inflation target: 2% on the CPI measure.
- The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of nine members sets Bank Rate at eight scheduled meetings a year. If CPI inflation is more than 1 percentage point away from the target, the Governor writes an open letter to the Chancellor explaining why and what the Bank will do.
- Transmission: a rise in Bank Rate raises market and lending rates, which reduces borrowing, consumption and investment, strengthens sterling and dampens inflation expectations. The effects take time, so the Bank looks ahead, roughly one to two years.
- The real interest rate is approximately the nominal rate minus expected inflation (the Fisher relation). What matters for spending is the real rate.
- The central bank's problem: choose the interest rate that minimises losses from inflation away from target and output away from potential, given the Phillips curve trade-off.
- At very low rates (Bank Rate was cut to 0.5% in March 2009 and 0.1% in March 2020), the Bank used quantitative easing: buying government bonds to lower long-term interest rates. It has since been reducing those holdings (quantitative tightening).

Where policy stands (at the time of writing, October 2026; check the Bank of England and ONS for later figures)
- Bank Rate was held at 3.75% on 17 September 2026, by six votes to three; the three dissenters preferred a rise to 4%. The next scheduled announcement is 5 November 2026.
- CPI inflation was 3.5% in September 2026, above the 2% target. With Bank Rate at 3.75%, the real rate measured against current inflation is only about 0.25%.
- Earlier, Bank Rate began rising from 0.1% in December 2021 and reached a peak of 5.25% in August 2023, in response to CPI inflation that peaked at 11.1% in October 2022.

Fiscal policy
- Fiscal policy uses government spending, taxes and transfers.
- Automatic stabilisers: in a downturn tax receipts fall and benefit payments rise without any decision, supporting demand; they work in reverse in a boom.
- Discretionary policy: deliberate changes, such as the temporary stimulus and job-support schemes used in 2020.
- The fiscal multiplier is larger when interest rates are stuck at their lower bound, when there is spare capacity and when spending goes to credit-constrained households.

Deficits and debt
- The deficit (public sector net borrowing) is a flow: the gap between spending and revenue in a year. The debt is a stock: the accumulation of past borrowing.
- The debt ratio rises with the primary deficit and with the gap between the interest rate and the growth rate: approximately, change in debt/GDP ≈ primary deficit + (r − g) × debt/GDP.
- Public sector net debt (excluding public sector banks) was provisionally £3,005.0 billion at the end of September 2026, about 94.0% of GDP, the first time it has exceeded £3 trillion. Borrowing from April to September 2026 was £97.8 billion, £6.0 billion more than the OBR had forecast (ONS, 21 October 2026).
- The OBR, created in 2010, produces the official economic and fiscal forecasts and assesses whether the government is on course to meet its fiscal rules.

Policy interactions
- Fiscal and monetary policy can work together, as in 2020, or pull in different directions, for example if a fiscal expansion leads the central bank to raise rates.
- Credibility matters: if people trust the central bank to hit its target, inflation expectations stay anchored and the cost of reducing inflation is lower.

Exam tips: explain the transmission mechanism step by step, distinguish deficit from debt, and date any UK figures you quote.

cards.b: Theory: accept any positive offer, so tiny offers are made. Evidence: offers commonly 40–50%; offers below about 20–30% are often rejected.
Substantive: judges the outcome itself. Procedural: judges how it was reached (voluntary exchange, fair competition, force).
The power to set the terms of an exchange, allowing the proposer to capture all the rent and leave the other party at their reservation option.
Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson, for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity.
A cost imposed on third parties that the decision-maker does not pay, so marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost and the market overproduces.
A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external damage at the efficient output, making the decision-maker internalise the externality.
With clear property rights and low bargaining costs, private bargaining can reach an efficient outcome regardless of who holds the rights (Coase, 1960).
Non-rival and non-excludable (e.g. street lighting); markets under-provide it because of free riding.
Rival but non-excludable (e.g. a fishery); tends to be overused. Ostrom (1990) showed community rules can manage some.
Hidden attributes: the party with less information attracts the 'wrong' trading partners, e.g. Akerlof's market for lemons (1970).
Hidden actions: one party changes behaviour after an agreement because the other cannot observe it, e.g. insured drivers taking less care.
A competitive equilibrium with no externalities and complete information is Pareto efficient.
Y = C + I + G + X − M.
Households spread consumption over time, basing it on expected lifetime income, so temporary income shocks change consumption little (if they can borrow and save).
1/(1 − c), where c is the marginal propensity to consume; c = 0.8 gives 5.
If everyone tries to save more at once, aggregate demand and incomes fall, so total saving may not rise.
It depends on expected future profits and confidence, which swing sharply over the cycle, and can be postponed.
Inflation rises above expected inflation when unemployment is below its equilibrium level, and falls when it is above.
3.5% (up from 3.1% in August), driven mainly by motor fuels (ONS, 21 October 2026). Figure at the time of writing (October 2026): check for updates.
2% on the CPI measure, set by the Chancellor; the Bank of England's MPC sets Bank Rate to meet it.
Nine members; sets Bank Rate at eight scheduled meetings a year; open letter to the Chancellor if CPI is more than 1 percentage point from target.

questions.q: A country's GDP per head grows at a steady 3.5% a year. Approximately how long does it take to double?
options: About 245 years
About 2,000 years
About 29 years
About 20 years
questions.why: By the rule of 70, 70/3.5 = 20 years (the exact figure is 20.1). 2,000 years divides 70 by 0.035, using the growth rate as a decimal when the rule needs it in percent. 29 years treats the growth as simple rather than compound interest: adding 3.5% of the starting level each year takes 100/3.5 ≈ 28.6 years to double. 245 years multiplies 70 by 3.5 instead of dividing.

questions.q: Four people have incomes of 10, 20, 30 and 40. What is the Gini coefficient?
questions.why: Cumulative shares are 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0, the area under the Lorenz curve is 0.375 and the Gini is 1 − 2 × 0.375 = 0.25. 0.375 is the area under the Lorenz curve itself, not the Gini. 0.75 is the Gini if one person had all the income. 0 would require everyone to have the same income.

questions.q: Explain what a Lorenz curve and a Gini coefficient show, and calculate the Gini coefficient for a population of four people with incomes 10, 20, 30 and 40.
markScheme: Lorenz curve: cumulative income share against cumulative population share, ranked from poorest; 45° line = equality
Gini = area between equality line and Lorenz curve ÷ area under equality line (0 to 1)
Cumulative shares 0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0
Area under Lorenz curve = 0.375 (trapezia of width 0.25)
Gini = 1 − 2 × 0.375 = 0.25, interpreted as moderate inequality
questions.modelAnswer: The Lorenz curve ranks people from poorest to richest and plots the cumulative share of income they receive against their cumulative share of the population. If incomes were equal it would be the 45° line; the further it sags below, the more unequal the distribution. The Gini coefficient is the area between the 45° line and the Lorenz curve divided by the total area under the 45° line (0.5), so it runs from 0 to 1. Total income is 100, so cumulative shares at 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of people are 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0. Using trapezia of width 0.25, the area under the Lorenz curve is 0.25 × [(0 + 0.1) + (0.1 + 0.3) + (0.3 + 0.6) + (0.6 + 1.0)]/2 = 0.375. Gini = (0.5 − 0.375)/0.5 = 0.25.

questions.q: A worker has utility u = c × t, where c is consumption and t is daily hours of free time, and earns w per hour, so c = w(24 − t). How many hours of free time does she choose?
options: 0, because consumption is always preferred
More free time the higher the wage
12, whatever the wage
questions.why: MRS = c/t and MRT = w, so c = wt; substituting into c = w(24 − t) gives t = 12, independent of w. 12w is her chosen consumption (c = w × 12), not her free time. Choosing no free time ignores that free time is valued: with u = c × t, zero free time gives zero utility. A rising demand for free time with the wage would require the income effect to outweigh the substitution effect, but here they cancel exactly.

questions.q: You can either work a shift paying £80 or go to a concert whose ticket costs £30. You choose the concert. What is the opportunity cost of going?
questions.why: The concert costs the £30 ticket plus the £80 of wages you give up, so the full opportunity cost is £110. £30 counts only the money spent. £80 counts only the forgone wage. £50 subtracts the ticket price from the wage, as if the two costs offset each other, when in fact both are given up.

questions.q: Using indifference curves and a feasible frontier, explain why a rise in the hourly wage has an ambiguous effect on the hours a person chooses to work.
markScheme: Feasible frontier c = w(24 − t) pivots and becomes steeper when w rises (MRT = w)
Optimum where MRS = MRT, tangency of indifference curve and frontier
Substitution effect: free time dearer, so less free time / more work
Income effect: higher real income, more free time if it is a normal good / less work
Net effect depends on which dominates; e.g. long-run fall in hours as wages rose
questions.modelAnswer: With 24 hours, free time t and wage w, the feasible frontier is c = w(24 − t), whose slope (the MRT) is w. The person chooses the point where an indifference curve is tangent to the frontier, so MRS = w. A wage rise makes the frontier steeper. The substitution effect, a movement along the original indifference curve to the new slope, reduces free time because each hour of leisure now costs more consumption. The income effect, a parallel shift to the higher curve, increases free time if it is a normal good, since the person is richer. The two pull in opposite directions, so hours worked may rise, fall or stay the same; the long-run fall in working hours as wages grew suggests the income effect has often dominated.

questions.q: A firm's product faces a price elasticity of demand of −4 and its marginal cost is constant at £12. What is its profit-maximising price?
questions.why: The markup rule (P − MC)/P = 1/4 gives P = MC/(1 − 1/4) = 12/0.75 = £16. £48 multiplies marginal cost by the elasticity, which is not what the rule says. £15 adds 25% to marginal cost, but the rule makes the markup 25% of the price, not of the cost. £12 is the competitive outcome P = MC, which applies only with perfectly elastic demand.

questions.q: In a one-shot public goods game, each of four players can contribute tokens to a pot that is multiplied by 1.6 and shared equally. For a purely self-interested player, what is the dominant strategy?
options: Contribute the same as the others, because that is the Nash equilibrium
Contribute half, to balance private and group payoffs
Contribute nothing, because each token contributed returns only 0.4 tokens to the contributor
Contribute everything, because the pot is multiplied by 1.6
questions.why: A token kept is worth 1, while a token contributed returns 1.6/4 = 0.4 to the contributor, so contributing nothing is best whatever others do. The multiplication by 1.6 makes contributing good for the group, not for the individual, which is exactly the social dilemma. Matching others is not a best response here: whatever they give, you gain by giving less. Contributing half has no basis for a self-interested player, since every token given lowers her own payoff.

questions.q: Explain why a firm might pay its workers more than their reservation wage, and how the level of unemployment affects the wage it needs to pay.
markScheme: Incomplete contract: effort cannot be fully specified or monitored (principal–agent problem)
Employment rent = value of job − value of reservation option; rent makes job loss costly
Higher wage → larger rent → more effort; firm chooses wage where extra effort per £ is maximised (efficiency wage)
Higher unemployment lowers the reservation option (longer expected spell without work)
So the firm can achieve the same effort with a lower wage; lower unemployment pushes wages up (wage-setting curve)
questions.modelAnswer: Employment contracts are incomplete: the firm cannot write down and enforce how hard someone works, so it faces a principal–agent problem. Paying a wage above the worker's reservation option creates an employment rent, the loss the worker would suffer if dismissed. The larger that rent, the more the worker has to lose by shirking, so effort rises with the wage, and the firm chooses the wage that gives the most effort per pound. When unemployment is high, a dismissed worker expects a longer and costlier spell without work, so the reservation option falls and the firm can obtain the same effort with a lower wage. When unemployment is low, firms must pay more, which is the logic behind an upward-sloping wage-setting curve.

questions.q: Demand is P = 100 − Q and supply is P = 20 + Q. A £10 per-unit tax is imposed on sellers. What price do buyers pay and what is the deadweight loss?
questions.why: The tax shifts supply to P = 30 + Q, so 100 − Q = 30 + Q gives Q = 35 and a buyer price of £65; quantity falls by 5, so the deadweight loss is ½ × 10 × 5 = £25. £70 and £50 assume buyers pay the whole tax on top of the old £60 price; demand would then fall to 30, giving a triangle of ½ × 10 × 10, but the sellers' price also falls, so buyers pay only £5 of the tax. £65 and £50 has the right price but forgets the ½ in the triangle area. £60 and £0 assumes the tax changes nothing, which is true only if one curve is perfectly inelastic.

questions.q: In the wage-setting and price-setting model of the labour market, what is the main effect of stronger competition between firms (lower markups)?
options: The wage-setting curve shifts up, raising the real wage and lowering employment
The price-setting curve shifts up, raising the real wage and equilibrium employment
Both curves shift down, so real wages fall
Nothing, because unemployment in equilibrium is always zero
questions.why: Lower markups mean firms charge less relative to wages, so the real wage consistent with their pricing rises: the price-setting curve moves up and equilibrium employment rises. Moving the wage-setting curve describes changes in workers' bargaining position, such as higher unemployment benefits, not product-market competition. Lower markups raise, not lower, the real wage, so a fall in real wages is the opposite of the prediction. Equilibrium in this model includes involuntary unemployment, which is what makes job loss costly.

questions.q: Demand for a good is P = 100 − Q and supply is P = 20 + Q. (a) Find the equilibrium and the consumer and producer surplus. (b) A £10 per-unit tax is levied on sellers. Find the new quantity, the prices paid by buyers and received by sellers, the tax revenue and the deadweight loss. Who bears the tax?
markScheme: (b) New supply P = 30 + Q; Q = 35
(b) Buyers pay £65, sellers receive £55
Incidence split equally (£5 each) because the curves have equal slopes; general point that the less elastic side bears more
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) 100 − Q = 20 + Q gives Q = 40 and P = 60. Consumer surplus is ½ × 40 × (100 − 60) = 800 and producer surplus ½ × 40 × (60 − 20) = 800.
(b) The tax raises sellers' required price by £10, so supply becomes P = 30 + Q. Then 100 − Q = 30 + Q gives Q = 35. Buyers pay 100 − 35 = £65 and sellers keep 65 − 10 = £55. Revenue is 10 × 35 = £350. Consumer and producer surplus each fall to 612.5, and the deadweight loss is ½ × 10 × (40 − 35) = £25, the value of the 5 lost trades. Buyers pay £5 more and sellers receive £5 less, so the burden is shared equally because the curves have equal slopes; in general, the less elastic side bears more.

questions.q: Which statement about Pareto efficiency is correct?
options: An allocation where one person has everything can be Pareto efficient
Any move from a Pareto-efficient allocation makes everyone worse off
A Pareto-efficient allocation is always fair
There is only one Pareto-efficient allocation in any economy
questions.why: If one person has everything, giving anything to someone else makes the owner worse off, so no Pareto improvement exists and the allocation is efficient. Fairness is a separate judgement, so efficiency does not guarantee it. There are usually many efficient allocations, differing in how the gains are divided. Leaving an efficient allocation makes at least one person worse off, not necessarily everyone; others may gain.

questions.q: In an ultimatum game over £100, which result is most consistent with typical experimental evidence?
options: Proposers usually offer £90 or more
Responders accept every offer above zero, but proposers offer half anyway
Proposers usually offer £40–£50 and offers of £10 are often rejected
Proposers usually offer £1 and responders accept it
questions.why: Experiments typically find offers of 40–50% and frequent rejection of very low offers, showing fairness norms and willingness to punish. Offering £1 and having it accepted is the prediction for purely self-interested players, not what is usually observed. Offers of £90 or more are rarely made, because proposers also care about their own payoff. Universal acceptance of positive offers contradicts the evidence that low offers are often rejected.

questions.q: Explain the difference between Pareto efficiency and fairness, using an example of how a change in the rules of the game could alter the outcome of an economic interaction.
markScheme: Pareto efficient: no feasible change makes someone better off without making someone worse off
Fairness: substantive (outcome) and/or procedural (process) judgement; separate from efficiency
Many efficient allocations exist, including very unequal ones
Example: a law (e.g. limiting hours or a minimum wage) or a change in bargaining power moves the outcome to a different, possibly more equal, allocation, which may still be efficient
questions.modelAnswer: An allocation is Pareto efficient if nobody can be made better off without making someone else worse off. Fairness is a value judgement about the outcome (substantive, for example how unequal incomes are) or about how it came about (procedural, for example whether exchange was voluntary). The two are distinct: an employer with take-it-or-leave-it power who pushes a worker down to their reservation option may reach a Pareto-efficient outcome in which the employer takes all the rent. A law that limits working hours or strengthens workers' bargaining power changes the rules, moving the outcome to another allocation in which the worker gets more of the surplus. The new outcome may also be efficient, but most people would judge it fairer.

questions.q: Demand is P = 100 − Q and the private marginal cost of production is 20 + Q. Each unit also causes £10 of external damage. What are the market quantity, the efficient quantity and the deadweight loss?
questions.why: The market sets demand equal to private cost, 100 − Q = 20 + Q, giving 40. The efficient quantity uses social cost, 100 − Q = 30 + Q, giving 35, and the deadweight loss is ½ × 10 × 5 = £25. The answer with an efficient quantity of 45 adds the £10 to the demand side instead of to cost, as if it were a positive externality. The answer giving 35 and 40 swaps the market and efficient quantities and also forgets the ½ in the triangle, giving £50. The answer with 40, 35 and £50 has the right quantities but makes the same mistake with the ½.

questions.q: A lighthouse's warning light can be seen by every ship nearby, and one ship seeing it does not reduce its usefulness to others. In what sense is it a public good?
options: It is non-rival but excludable
It is provided by the government
It is rival but non-excludable
It is non-rival and non-excludable
questions.why: One ship's use does not reduce others' (non-rival) and ships cannot be stopped from seeing the light (non-excludable), which defines a pure public good. Rival but non-excludable describes a common-pool resource such as a fishery. Non-rival but excludable describes a club good, such as a subscription streaming service. Who provides a good does not define it: many public goods are publicly funded, but the definition rests on rivalry and excludability.

questions.q: Explain, with a diagram, why a market with a negative production externality is inefficient, and compare a Pigouvian tax with Coasean bargaining as remedies.
markScheme: Diagram: demand, private MC, social MC above private MC by the external cost
Market output where demand = private MC exceeds efficient output where demand = social MC
Deadweight loss triangle between social MC and demand over the excess output
Pigouvian tax = marginal external damage at efficient output internalises the cost; needs information on damage, raises revenue
Coase: with clear property rights and low transaction costs, bargaining achieves efficiency; fails with many parties/high bargaining costs/asymmetric information
questions.modelAnswer: Draw demand (marginal benefit), the private marginal cost curve and a social marginal cost curve that lies above it by the external damage per unit. The market produces where demand meets private marginal cost, but the efficient output is lower, where demand meets social marginal cost. Each extra unit between the two quantities costs society more than it is worth, giving a deadweight loss triangle between social marginal cost and demand. A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external damage at the efficient output raises the private cost to the social cost, so the market chooses the efficient quantity and the government gains revenue; the difficulty is measuring the damage. Coase showed that if property rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, the polluter and those affected can negotiate the efficient outcome without government. But when many people are affected (as with air pollution), bargaining costs are high, information is private or the victims are poor, bargaining fails, which is why taxes, permits or regulation are usually used.

questions.q: The marginal propensity to consume out of disposable income is 0.8, the tax rate is 25% and the marginal propensity to import is 0.2. What is the multiplier?
options: About 1.67
questions.why: The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.8 × 0.75 + 0.2) = 1/0.6 ≈ 1.67. 5 is the simple multiplier 1/(1 − 0.8), which ignores both taxes and imports. 2.5 leaves out one of the two leakages: allowing for tax but not imports gives 1/(1 − 0.6) = 2.5, and allowing for imports but not tax gives 1/(1 − 0.8 + 0.2) = 2.5 as well. 0.6 is the denominator, the share of each extra pound of income that leaks out, rather than its reciprocal.

questions.q: During a recession all households decide to save a larger share of their income. According to the paradox of thrift, what is the likely result?
options: Output and incomes fall, so total saving may not increase
Total saving rises by the amount households intended
Interest rates must rise because saving has increased
Output is unaffected because saving equals investment automatically
questions.why: Higher saving means lower consumption, which cuts aggregate demand, output and incomes; with lower incomes, total saving may end up unchanged or lower. Assuming saving rises as planned ignores the fall in income that spending cuts cause. In this model, weaker demand puts downward rather than upward pressure on interest rates. Saving and investment are equal after the fact because income adjusts to make them equal, which is exactly the mechanism by which output falls.

questions.q: Explain the multiplier process and calculate the effect on GDP of a £10 billion rise in government spending when the marginal propensity to consume out of disposable income is 0.8, the tax rate is 25% and the marginal propensity to import is 0.2. Why might the actual effect be smaller?
markScheme: Process: extra spending → higher incomes → more consumption → further income rises (successive rounds)
Leakages through taxes, saving and imports shrink each round
ΔGDP ≈ £16.7 billion
Smaller in practice: crowding out via higher interest rates/monetary response, Ricardian or precautionary saving, capacity constraints
questions.modelAnswer: Government spending of £10 billion raises the incomes of those who supply the goods. They spend part of the extra income after tax on domestic output, raising others' incomes, and so on through successive rounds. Each round is smaller because of leakages: 25% goes in tax, 20% of the remaining spending goes on imports and 20% of disposable income is saved. The multiplier is 1/(1 − c(1 − t) + m) = 1/(1 − 0.6 + 0.2) = 1/0.6 ≈ 1.67, so GDP rises by about £16.7 billion. The actual effect may be smaller if the central bank raises interest rates in response, crowding out investment; if households save more because they expect higher future taxes or feel uncertain; or if the economy is near capacity, so prices rise rather than output.

questions.q: The Bank of England's MPC announced on 17 September 2026 that Bank Rate would be:
options: Held at 5.25%, its 2023 peak
Held at 3.75%, with three members voting for a rise to 4%
Cut to 3.5% to support growth
Raised to 4% because CPI inflation was 3.5%
questions.why: The MPC voted 6–3 to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%, with the minority preferring 4%. A cut to 3.5% is the wrong direction, since rising inflation led some members to argue for a rise. A rise to 4% was the minority view, not the decision. 5.25% was the peak reached in August 2023, long since reduced.

questions.q: Government debt is 90% of GDP, the nominal interest rate on debt is 4% and nominal GDP grows at 3%. Approximately what primary balance keeps the debt ratio constant?
options: A balanced primary budget
A primary deficit of about 0.9% of GDP
A primary surplus of about 0.9% of GDP
A primary surplus of 1% of GDP
questions.why: The debt ratio is stable when the primary surplus equals (r − g) × debt ratio = (0.04 − 0.03) × 90% = 0.9% of GDP. A primary deficit gets the sign wrong: with r above g the government must run a surplus just to stand still. 1% forgets to multiply the interest–growth gap by the debt ratio. A balanced primary budget would let the debt ratio rise, because interest costs grow faster than GDP.

questions.q: Explain how a rise in Bank Rate is expected to reduce inflation, and why the Bank of England has to look ahead when setting policy.
markScheme: Higher Bank Rate raises market lending rates (mortgages, loans) and returns on saving
Reduces consumption and investment (and asset prices), lowering aggregate demand
Stronger sterling lowers import prices; lower demand raises unemployment, easing wage and price pressure (Phillips curve)
Anchors inflation expectations if the Bank is credible
Lags of roughly 1–2 years mean policy must respond to forecast inflation, not current inflation
questions.modelAnswer: When Bank Rate rises, banks raise the interest rates on mortgages, loans and savings. Borrowing becomes more expensive and saving more rewarding, so households cut consumption and firms postpone investment; higher rates also lower asset prices, reducing wealth. Sterling tends to strengthen, making imports cheaper. Lower aggregate demand raises unemployment above its equilibrium level, weakening workers' bargaining power, so wage and price inflation fall along the Phillips curve. If the Bank is credible, people expect inflation to return to 2%, which itself restrains wage and price setting. These effects take roughly one to two years to work through, so the MPC must set rates according to where it expects inflation to be, not where it is today.

questions.q:
A competitive market has demand P = 100 − Q and private marginal cost (supply) P = 20 + Q, where Q is in thousands of units and P is in pounds. Production causes pollution costing £10 per unit to people living nearby.
(a) Find the market equilibrium and the efficient (socially optimal) output. [4]
(b) Calculate the deadweight loss from the externality. [3]
(c) Show that a Pigouvian tax achieves the efficient output, and find the price buyers pay, the price sellers receive and the tax revenue. [5]
(d) Explain why the efficient outcome could, in principle, be reached by bargaining between the firm and the residents, and why this is unlikely in practice. [4]
(e) Discuss one other policy that could address the externality and compare it with the tax. [4]
markScheme: (a) Market: 100 − Q = 20 + Q → Q = 40, P = 60. Social MC = 30 + Q → efficient Q = 35, P = 65
(b) DWL = ½ × 10 × (40 − 35) = 25 (thousand £, given units)
(c) Tax of £10 per unit = marginal external damage shifts private MC to social MC; Q = 35
(c) Buyers pay £65, sellers receive £55, revenue = 10 × 35 = 350 (thousand £)
(d) Coase: clear property rights and low bargaining costs allow the parties to agree on the efficient output whoever holds the rights
(d) In practice: many residents, free riding, bargaining/information costs, unequal wealth or power
(e) Valid alternative (quota/regulation, tradable permits, technology standards) with comparison: certainty of quantity vs price, information needs, cost-effectiveness, revenue
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The market ignores the pollution, so 100 − Q = 20 + Q gives Q = 40 (thousand units) and P = £60. Social marginal cost is private cost plus £10: 30 + Q. The efficient output sets 100 − Q = 30 + Q, so Q = 35 and the corresponding price is £65.

(b) The 5 thousand units between 35 and 40 each cost society more than they are worth. The gap between social marginal cost and demand is 0 at Q = 35 and 10 at Q = 40, so the deadweight loss is ½ × 10 × 5 = 25, that is £25,000 since Q is in thousands.

(c) A Pigouvian tax of £10 per unit, equal to the marginal damage, raises private marginal cost to 30 + Q, so the market produces where 100 − Q = 30 + Q, Q = 35, which is efficient. Buyers pay £65, sellers receive £65 − £10 = £55, and revenue is £10 × 35,000 = £350,000. The burden is shared equally between buyers (£5 more) and sellers (£5 less) because the curves have equal slopes. The revenue could be used to compensate residents or reduce other taxes.

(d) Coase (1960) argued that if property rights are clearly defined and bargaining is costless, the parties will agree the efficient output. If residents have the right to clean air, the firm will pay them to accept pollution only up to the point where its gain equals their damage; if the firm has the right to pollute, residents will pay it to cut output from 40 to 35, since each unit cut is worth £10 to them but less than £10 to the firm. Either way output ends up at 35, although who pays differs. In practice there are many residents, each with an incentive to free ride on others' payments, the damage is hard to measure, negotiation is costly, and residents may lack the wealth to pay, so bargaining is unlikely to succeed.

(e) The regulator could set a quota of 35,000 units or issue 35,000 tradable pollution permits. A quota gives certainty about the quantity of pollution, which matters when damage rises sharply beyond a threshold, but the regulator needs to know the efficient quantity and, with several firms, a fixed quota may not allocate cuts to those who can make them most cheaply. Tradable permits fix the quantity while letting firms trade, so reductions happen where they are cheapest, as in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme. A tax fixes the price of pollution and raises revenue but leaves the quantity uncertain if the regulator misjudges the cost curves. With a constant marginal damage of £10, as here, the tax is the natural instrument because it matches the damage exactly.

questions.q: "With inflation above target in 2026, the Bank of England should raise interest rates and the government should cut borrowing." Discuss, using the models of the course and current UK evidence.
markScheme: Sets out the current facts accurately and dated: CPI 3.5% in September 2026 (target 2%), driven by motor fuels; Bank Rate held at 3.75% on 17 Sep 2026 (6–3); PSND about 94% of GDP; borrowing above OBR forecast
Explains the transmission mechanism of monetary policy and the Phillips curve trade-off, including lags
Distinguishes a supply (energy) shock from excess demand and explains the policy dilemma (higher inflation with weaker output)
Discusses expectations and credibility: second-round effects on wages and prices justify tightening if expectations rise
Analyses fiscal consolidation: lowers demand and inflation pressure, improves debt dynamics (r − g), but multiplier effects and pro-cyclical risk
Considers policy mix/coordination and that both tightening together may overdo it
Reaches a reasoned, conditional conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
At the time of writing (October 2026), CPI inflation was 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August and well above the 2% target, with motor fuels the largest contributor (ONS, 21 October 2026). On 17 September the MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75%, but three of the nine members voted to raise it to 4%. Public sector net debt had just passed £3 trillion, about 94% of GDP, and borrowing in the first half of 2026/27 was £6 billion above the OBR's forecast. So the statement reflects a real debate.

The case for raising interest rates rests on the transmission mechanism. A higher Bank Rate raises borrowing costs, reduces consumption and investment, strengthens sterling and lowers demand; with unemployment above its equilibrium level, wage and price pressure eases along the Phillips curve. Because policy works with a lag of a year or more, the Bank must act on forecast inflation.

But the source of inflation matters. A rise in fuel prices is a supply shock: it raises prices and squeezes real incomes, which already weakens demand. Raising rates cannot lower the world oil price; it can only reduce inflation by cutting domestic demand and employment. If the shock is temporary, the standard advice is to look through its first-round effect. The key question is second-round effects: if workers demand higher wages to make up for lost real income and firms raise prices in turn, inflation expectations could drift up. Then a rate rise is justified to protect the credibility that keeps expectations anchored. The 6–3 vote shows how finely balanced this judgement is.

On fiscal policy, cutting borrowing would reduce aggregate demand and so help the Bank. It would also stabilise the debt ratio: when the interest rate on debt exceeds the growth rate, the government needs a primary surplus of roughly (r − g) times the debt ratio just to keep debt stable, and higher rates make that harder. Against this, the multiplier means consolidation reduces output, and tightening both policies during a supply shock risks recession. Automatic stabilisers should be allowed to work. The policy mix matters: if the government tightens credibly, the Bank may need to raise rates less.

Conclusion: the statement is defensible only conditionally. A modest rise in rates is justified if there is evidence that expectations and wage growth are responding to the fuel shock, and gradual, credible fiscal consolidation is sensible given high debt and rising interest costs. Sharp simultaneous tightening in response to a temporary supply shock would risk an avoidable downturn.
